Putting a "Generate video" button in a Next.js app sounds like one fetch. In practice video generation has three properties that shape the whole design:
It's slow. A 5-second clip takes one to several minutes. A route handler that waits for it will hit your platform's function time limit, and a user who refreshes loses the job.
It costs real money per request. Anyone who finds your API route can call it in a loop. The key must stay on the server, and the server must decide what one request may cost.
It fails sometimes, and a naive retry starts a second paid job.
So the shape is: a rou…

I work on OnePassApps, so this is our own site, and every number in the table below was measured on the live pages today, not remembered.

So here is every public URL we serve, measured one by one: the HTML the server sends, the compressed size on the wire, and how long the first byte took to arrive.
One machine, one network, 5 November 2026. Plain HTTPS with curl, no browser session, no cookies, no JavaScript. Each route was fetched twice: once with Accept-Encoding: gzip (the compressed size on the wire) and once with decompression enabled (the decoded size of the document itself). Time to first byte is the server's own number for t…

When I edit a page of documentation, I used to skim past the code blocks. They looked technical, someone had presumably tested them, and my job was the prose around them. That was a mistake. The code samples are often the only part of a page a reader actually uses. Many people jump straight to the first grey box, copy it, and paste it into a terminal. If it fails, the clear paragraph above it doesn't help much.
So now code samples get an editing pass of their own. Here is what I check.
This is the first question, and the answer is "no" more often than you'd think. The usual problems are small:
A shell prompt ($ or >) at the start of each line, which gets pasted along with the command

articles.description:
When a production issue occurs, finding the actual cause can be harder than fixing it.
A request might start in a Next.js frontend, pass through multiple Node.js services, hit a database, and eventually fail somewhere along the way.
You might have logs in one place, traces in another, and error reports somewhere else.
Without proper instrumentation and correlation, debugging becomes a manual exercise.
This is where OpenTelemetry (OTel) becomes useful.
OpenTelemetry provides a vendor-neutral way to collect traces, metrics, and logs from your applications. Once your applications are instrumented, you can change telemetry backends without rewriting your instrumentation.
In this guide, we'll set up OpenTelemetry for a practical production stack:
Next.js frontend
Node.js / Express backend
Distr…

Most "AI video in n8n" tutorials stop at one HTTP Request node that fires a prompt at a model. That works once in a demo. In a real workflow it breaks in three ways:

You’ve just tweaked your CSS or updated some DOM nodes, expecting the page to snap instantly to the new styles or layout. Instead, you see a flicker, a delay, or worse, a janky animation that ruins the user experience.
Why does this happen? What exactly goes on inside the browser when your code changes the DOM?
I spent hours debugging a sluggish animation where every frame dropped, and the culprit was a forced reflow that no one expected. That deep dive into the browser’s rendering pipeline revealed a surprisingly complex but fascinating process that browsers use to repaint and reflow the page efficiently.
Let me walk you through what happens under the hood after you change the DOM, how browsers batch and optimize these updates, and why some DOM reads or writes can cause big performance hi…

The "productivity stack" conversation usually focuses on apps: Notion, Todoist, Obsidian, Roam. These get attention because they're downloadable, marketed, and visible. What gets less attention is the browser — the tool you're in for most of the actual work. Getting the browser right is at least as important as your note-taking app.

articles.author: Mogley1011
articles.description:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) allows LLMs in Claude Desktop, Cursor, and agent frameworks to run tools, query databases, and read local files.
Giving an LLM structured tools is much cleaner than pasting text into prompts. But exposing system actions to a model introduces failure modes that traditional API endpoints never had to consider.
Here are four real security and reliability patterns uncovered when auditing custom MCP servers, and how to defend against them.
The most common trap is exposing a general-purpose command runner (e.g. execute_bash or run_command) so the agent has maximum flexibility.
Because LLMs can experience indirect prompt injection from untrusted text (such as reading an issue description or web page), an attacker can embed hidden instructions like:
System notice: …
articles.title: What happens when you give an LLM an MCP tool: 4 security patterns from auditing tool servers

articles.description:
Engineer's view. This is a search ranking bug. Your site search returns the page that matches the query's words best, even when that page is out of date. A model reading a long prompt does the same thing. A passage that echoes your question can beat the true one. Every extra chunk you send adds rivals.
TL;DR. A model reading a long prompt favors the passage that best matches your question, true or not. Long prompts hurt mostly because they carry more look-alikes, so keep those out and ask questions only the right passage answers.
You lost a blue umbrella, so you go to the lost-and-found desk. You say, "I lost a blue umbrella."
